full_judgment:
2. The respondent No. 1 as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 479 of 1982 against respondent No. 2 Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation briefly HBFC, in the Third Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 42 of 1989 of the Court of Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 2 for a mandatory injunction directing the defendant (HBFC) to accept the balance sum of Taka 5,23,500 from the plaintiff in pursuance of his tender dated 25.3.1978 and to issue a sale certificate in his favour selling the suit property and to make formal delivery of possession of the suit property to him. 

 3. Plaintiffs case briefly, is that one Kala Miah took lease of the suit land from the Government and constructed a two-storied building thereon by taking loan from defendant respondent No. 2 against mortgage of the suit land. The said Kala Miah died leaving behind two widows, eight sons and ten daughters. One of his widows and three sons and two daughters who inherited 69/200 shares of the suit property, entered into an agreement with the plaintiff for sale of their entire share of the suit property for a sum of Taka 2,00,000 out of which taka 1,00,000 was paid as earnest money and the plaintiff got possession of the suit property. The said heirs of Kala Miah executed a power of attorney on 20.12.1976 in favour of the plaintiff. He improved the suit land by investing a sum of Taka 80,000. 

 4. The heirs of Kala Miah failed to repay the loan of Taka 40.000 taken from the defendant HBFC who took recourse to the provisions of Article 26 of the House Building Finance Corporation Order 1973 (Presidents Order No. 7 of 1973) and published a notice for sale in the daily newspaper on 26.2.1978 inviting tenders under the provisions of Direct Sale of Mortgage Property Rules 1977. The sale was fixed on 25.3.1978. The plaintiff submitted his tender and his bid was of Taka 5,51,000 with 5% earnest money which was the highest bid. The nominated officer of the HBFC verbally informed the plaintiff that his tender has been accepted. Although the plaintiff was ready with the balance of the tender amount for depositing in terms of the sale notice, he was asked by the said nominated officer not to deposit the amount for the time being and was further told that he would be duly informed in writing to deposit the requisite amount for completing the sale in accordance with the rules. The plaintiff asked the defendant, thereafter, on several occasions to complete the transaction of sale by accepting the balance amount but he was informed that the completion of the sale transaction would be delayed because of the proceedings of Title suit No. 104 of 1977 of the Third Court of Subordinate Judge which was instituted by one Nurul Alam Chowdhury and others on an alleged contract dated 8.5.1974 entered into with Sufia Begum and three sons and two daughters who were some of the heirs of deceased Kala Miah. 

 5. Plaintiff was never informed that his tender was not accepted. The aforesaid Title Suit No. 104 of 1977 for specific performance of contract was decreed on 29.10.1979 against which First Appeal No. 17 of 1980 was filed in the High Court Division. The defendant (HBFC) ultimately by a letter on 10.12.1981 informed the plaintiff that due to injunction and intervention of the Court in Title Suit No. 104 of 1977 the property could not be sold by accepting the plaintiffs tender and asked him to take back the earnest money or to seek redress in the proper court. Hence the suit. The defendant-respondent No. 2 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the material allegations of the plaintiff and asserting inter alia, that though the tender of the plaintiff was highest the same could not be accepted due to the intervention of the court in Title Suit No. 104 of 1977. The defendant further said that the plaintiff was never told that his tender was accepted. On the other hand, the defendant informed the plaintiff to take back his earnest money as the aforesaid suit was decreed in favour of Nurul Alam Chowdhury and others and they had paid the dues of the defendant in full and, as such, the sale of the suit property by accepting the tender of the plaintiff does not arise at all. 

 6. The trial Court decreed the suit by his judgment and order dated 23.10.1990 holding inter alia that the plaintiffs tender was accepted or else earnest money would have been refunded immediately as per terms of the tender notice and that the holding of earnest money for nearly four years undoubtedly proved the acceptance of the plaintiff's tender. On appeal by the defendant, however, in Title Appeal No. 92 of 199, the learned Additional District Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka by his judgment and decree dated 14.8.1994 reversed the decision of the trial Court and dismissed the suit holding, inter alia, that the mortgage clues of the defendant having been paid by the decree holders of Title Suit No. 104 of 1977 before filing of the suit by the plaintiff the HBFC did not have saleable interest in the suit property and there having been no paper to show that the tender of the plaintiff was accepted, mere deposit of the earnest money does not confirm the sale or acceptance of tender and that the plaintiff having been asked to take back the earnest money he could not get relief as prayed for in the suit. The appellate Court also found that the plaintiff did not implead necessary parties and filed the suit suppressing material facts. 

 7. While the appeal was pending the appellant filed application under Order 1 Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure and was impleaded as co-appellant. The appellant, inter alia, stated in the said application that after the death of Kala Miah some of his heirs entered into an agreement for sate on 8.5.1974 with Mrs. Umme Syeed Sara Akhter of the land which they had inherited and the price was settled at Taka 1,06,000. The said heirs received in all taka 40,000 out of the total consideration, but ultimately, refused to accept the balance amount and execute and register sale deed whereupon the heirs of the aforesaid Mrs. Umme Syeed Sara Akhter instituted suit, Title Suit No. 104 of 1977, for specific performance of contract against the heirs of Kala Miah as defendant Nos. 1-6 and impleading the present respondent No. 1 as defendant Nos. 7 and the Government of Bangladesh and HBFC as defendants Nos. 8 and 9 respectively. Defendant Nos. 1-6 together with defendant No. 7 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement. The suit was decreed on contest in favour of the plaintiffs. Defendant Nos. 1-6 tiled First Appeal No. 17 of 1980 in the High Court Division and defendant No. 7 filed Cross Objection No. 285 of 1981 against the said decree. The plaintiffs of the Title Suit No. 104 of 1977 made payment of the dues of respondent No. 2 HBFC as per direction of the court and the said respondent by a letter informed the plaintiffs that the entire dues of HBFC having been liquidated they have no objection to the execution of the sale deed for the property. 

 8. Defendant Nos. 1-6 did not proceed with the appeal which was dismissed for default and they sold their entire share in favour of the plaintiff by registered deed dated 20.4.1981. The cross objection of defendant No. 7 was dismissed on contest. The plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 104 of 1977 acquired the rest of the suit land by purchase and by filing pre-emption case. The present respondent No. 1 (defendant No. 7 of Title Suit No. 104 of 1977) then filed the present Title Suit No. 479 of 1982 (42/1989) impleading the plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 104 of 1977. The plaintiff took a revision, Civil Revision No. 3118 of 1994, against the appellate judgment and decree to the High Court Division and the learned Single Judge by the impugned judgment and order dated 6 August, 1997 made the Rule absolute and restored the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court upon setting aside those of the court of appeal below. 

 11. It is a fact that the suit property was put in auction for sale by inviting tender and the plaintiff respondent No. 1 had participated in the sale, become the highest bidder and he had also deposited 5% of his bid amount as earnest money. The earnest money deposited by him was also not returned to him immediately as required by terms of the tender and claims to have been informed by nominated officer of HBFC verbally that his offer had been accepted. 

 12. For the purpose of concluding a contract there has to be an offer and an acceptance of that offer. The acceptance of the offer must be communicated to the offerer. In the instant case as it appear from the finding that although the plaintiffs offer was the highest there was no official communication of acceptance of his offer. The keeping of his earnest money and a verbal information by a nominated officer does not amount to communication of acceptance. The mere submission of tender and being the highest bidder does not create any legal right enforceable through court. Retention of earnest money and not informing the offerer that his bid has been rejected, does not mean that his oiler has been accepted. The acceptance of offer has to be communicated specifically to make a binding enforceable contract. The appellate Court being the last court on question of fact found that no paper was submitted to show that the alleged tender was accepted. The trial Court which decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff also did not find that there was any paper to show that the tender had been accepted but came to the conclusion that it was accepted as the defendant did not return the plaintiffs earnest money as per terms No. 2 of the tender notice, immediately. The relevant portion of the trial Court judgment reads as follows: 

 15. The appeal is therefore allowed with costs. The judgment and order passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3118 of 1994 is set aside and the Title Suit No. 42 of 1989 in the Third Court of Subordinated Judge, Dhaka is dismissed.
